title: IT Spending Pulse: AI Takes Priority as Confidence Returns
gist: A May 2026 BCG survey of 423 director-level-plus IT buyers in North America and Europe shows enterprise IT budget growth accelerating to 5.8% for 2026 (up 2.2 points from what was planned mid-2025), but the growth is narrowly concentrated: 66% plan to raise AI/ML spending while most other categories — CRM, ERP, IT services — go net negative. AI is the only category where buyers plan to add vendors (net 34%), and measured GenAI ROI has risen to 13.8%, with high-maturity firms at ~19% versus 8%–9% for laggards.

insights.claim: Enterprise IT leaders now expect total IT spending to grow 5.8% in 2026 versus 2025, the strongest outlook in the two-year history of BCG's IT Spending Pulse survey and 2.2 percentage points above the 3.6% they were planning for 2026 as of mid-2025.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: An upward revision of this size in forward IT budgets is a leading indicator for enterprise software, cloud, and IT hardware revenue guidance into 2026 — bias toward beats in AI-adjacent vendors.
insights.quote: IT leaders now expect overall spending to grow 5.8% in 2026 compared with 2025—the strongest outlook the survey has recorded
insights.locator: Confidence Returns, and Budgets Follow

insights.claim: IT budget expectations bottomed at 2.4% growth immediately after the early-2025 tariff announcements, but firms then spent more freely than planned in H2 2025, delivering actual 2025 growth of 4.6% — in line with pre-tariff optimism.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Tariff-driven IT spending guidance cuts proved to be a head-fake; treat future macro-shock-driven IT budget guide-downs as likely over-corrections that get spent back within two to three quarters.
insights.quote: Firms then spent through the second half of the year more freely than they had planned, bringing actual 2025 growth to 4.6%
insights.locator: That figure is notable not only for its size

insights.claim: IT buyer sentiment has functioned as a real-time barometer of the broader economy over two years — exuberance in December 2024, austerity by April 2025 when tariffs pushed cost control level with growth as the top priority, cautious rebalancing by mid-2025, and conviction-led concentration by May 2026.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Use the IT Spending Pulse oscillation pattern as a sentiment proxy for corporate capex appetite ahead of reported enterprise tech results.
insights.quote: Two years of the IT Spending Pulse have read like a barometer of the broader economy.
insights.locator: Two years of the IT Spending Pulse

insights.claim: AI capability maturity is itself driving the budget cycle: since mid-2025 the share of firms self-describing as high-maturity AI adopters (AI embedded in enterprise strategy and scaled across multiple functions) rose 10.8 percentage points, and medium-maturity firms rose 4.7 points.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Spending is a function of demonstrated capability, not hype — the pool of firms able to absorb large AI budgets is mechanically expanding, supporting multi-year rather than one-year demand.
insights.quote: As capabilities improve, so does the willingness to invest behind them.
insights.locator: Underlying the numbers is a steady climb in AI maturity

themes.theme: Concentration: AI Cannibalizes the Rest of the Stack

insights.claim: Across the full technology stack, IT buyers expect net spending to DECLINE in most product categories over the next 12 months, with AI/ML, cloud, and security the only meaningful exceptions.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Headline IT budget growth of 5.8% masks a zero-sum reallocation — non-AI software names face a shrinking wallet even in an expanding market; avoid reading aggregate IT growth as a rising tide.
insights.quote: Across the full technology stack, buyers expect net spending to decline in most product categories over the next 12 months.
insights.locator: AI Draws Spending Away from Everything Else

insights.claim: 66% of surveyed IT buyers expect to increase spending on AI and machine learning including GenAI and AI agents — more than any other category and up 21 percentage points from mid-2025.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A 21-point jump in six months is the steepest category acceleration in the survey — a direct demand signal for AI model, agent, and ML platform vendors.
insights.locator: The exceptions are telling

insights.claim: Cloud services (up 11 points) and security infrastructure (up 3 points) are the second and third largest gainers in buyer spending intent, explicitly because they are the enablers AI depends on for running applications at volume and keeping data environments secure.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Cloud and security are the highest-conviction second-order AI beneficiaries in this dataset — they get pulled along by AI budgets rather than competing with them.
insights.quote: the enablers that AI depends on for running AI applications at volume and keeping data environments secure
insights.locator: The next largest gainers are the enablers

insights.claim: CRM and ERP spending intent turned negative again after showing brief momentum in earlier survey waves, as companies reprioritized around building AI capability rather than modernizing systems of record.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The core systems-of-record modernization cycle is being deferred by AI budgets — a direct negative read-through for CRM/ERP license and migration revenue.
insights.quote: companies reprioritized around building AI capability rather than modernizing systems of record
insights.locator: Almost all other tech investments are losing ground

insights.claim: IT services spending intent swung down 19 points versus H2 2025, but this reflects reprioritized budget growth rather than insourcing — over the past three years 44% of respondents outsourced somewhat or much more versus just 4% who brought meaningfully more work in-house.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Do not read the IT services sentiment collapse as a structural insourcing threat to service providers; it is budget crowd-out, which can reverse when AI programs need implementation muscle.
insights.quote: buyers aren’t pulling work back in-house or cutting ties with providers
insights.locator: IT services saw a meaningful reversal

insights.claim: When asked where they intend to expand versus consolidate suppliers, IT buyers pointed to net consolidation in every category except AI and ML, where a net 34% plan to expand their roster of providers.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: AI is the only enterprise tech category where new entrants can still win seats at scale; everywhere else, incumbents gain share and challengers get squeezed out of the vendor list.
insights.quote: AI and ML stand alone, with a net 34% of buyers planning to expand their roster of providers.
insights.locator: When asked where they intend to expand versus consolidate

insights.claim: Cloud, analytics, and security are seeing continued spending growth delivered through a stable or shrinking set of vendors as buyers pragmatically simplify their portfolios.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Rising budgets plus falling vendor counts equals share concentration — favor scaled platform incumbents in cloud, analytics, and security over point-solution challengers.
insights.locator: Cloud, analytics, and security see continued spending

themes.theme: From Pilot Sprawl to Disciplined Execution

insights.claim: The average number of GenAI and AI-agent use cases per respondent has fallen across every maturity tier, even as adoption of priority use cases — analytics, customer service, security and risk prevention, and internal communications — has climbed.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Narrowing use-case breadth means spend is consolidating into a handful of deep workloads — winners will be vendors embedded in analytics, service, and security workflows, not generic horizontal AI tools.
insights.quote: The strategy has shifted from spraying pilots across the organization to executing on what is core.
insights.locator: From Experimentation to Disciplined Execution

insights.claim: Weighted-average measured ROI on GenAI and AI-agent deployments has risen to 13.8%, up 2.6 points from 11.2% in the mid-2025 survey.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A hard, improving enterprise ROI number is the strongest available rebuttal to the 'AI capex has no payback' bear case — watch whether the series keeps compounding each survey wave.
insights.locator: That discipline is showing up in returns

insights.claim: Much of the improvement in average GenAI ROI comes from a changing mix of respondents — more firms now sit in higher-maturity segments that report stronger returns — rather than purely from better returns at constant maturity.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The aggregate ROI improvement is partly a composition effect; don't extrapolate it as evidence that any given deployment is getting more profitable — check maturity-adjusted returns.
insights.quote: Much of that gain reflects a changing mix of respondents
insights.locator: That discipline is showing up in returns

themes.theme: The Maturity Gap and Token Economics

insights.claim: High AI maturity firms report measured ROI of roughly 19%, more than double the 8% to 9% reported by little-to-no-maturity and low-maturity adopters, and early experimentation among less mature firms still produces a meaningful share of negative or unclear returns.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: AI returns are bimodal, not average — the addressable market for AI spend that actually compounds is concentrated in a leader cohort, which should drive vendor revenue concentration too.
insights.quote: discipline and scale are what convert investment into value
insights.locator: A Widening Gap Between Leaders and Laggards

insights.claim: Counterintuitively, the firms with the best visibility into AI and token costs — often at team- and user-level granularity — use that visibility to be MORE permissive, adopting liberal token strategies that encourage developers to use AI tools freely rather than throttling them.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Better cost instrumentation expands rather than caps token consumption — bullish for inference volume, and a tailwind for AI cost-observability/FinOps tooling vendors.
insights.quote: Counterintuitively, these firms use that visibility to be more permissive, adopting liberal token strategies that encourage developers to use AI tools freely rather than throttling them.
insights.locator: Maturity confers advantages beyond returns

insights.claim: At high-maturity firms the top 10% of AI adopters — the power users — reportedly generate outsized productivity without consuming a disproportionate share of spending, which the author treats as the signature of effective token usage.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Use the ratio of power-user productivity to power-user token spend as a diagnostic for whether an enterprise AI program is compounding or just burning inference budget.
insights.quote: their power users—the top 10% of AI adopters—reportedly generate outsized productivity without consuming a disproportionate share of spending
insights.locator: They can afford to

insights.claim: Less-mature firms lack team- and user-level AI cost visibility and therefore default to hard usage limits and cautious, tactical management — a self-reinforcing constraint that caps their returns.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Throttling is a symptom of missing instrumentation, not of cost discipline; laggard AI budgets will stay structurally smaller until observability is solved.
insights.locator: Less-mature firms reportedly lack that visibility

insights.claim: The differentiator among AI leaders is not spending magnitude but active tracking and allocation — leaders 'are not simply spending more,' they make active decisions to ensure tokens are spent effectively and concentrate bets on what is truly core to the business.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Screen portfolio companies on AI spend governance, not AI spend level — announced AI budgets alone are a poor predictor of realized returns.
insights.quote: The takeaway is that the leaders are not simply spending more. They are actively tracking where spending is going and making active decisions to ensure tokens are spent effectively.
insights.locator: The takeaway is that the leaders

insights.claim: The May 2026 wave surveyed 423 director-level-or-above respondents (285 North America, 138 Europe) at mid-size and large companies across technology, financial services, industrial goods, health care, retail, energy, and education, with prior waves at N=434 (July 2025), N=313 (April 2025), and N=602 (December 2024).
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Sample sizes vary materially wave to wave (313 to 602), so period-over-period point changes in this series carry non-trivial composition noise — weight the direction more than the decimal.
insights.locator: Survey Methodology
